<a id="entry-feat-init-repo-feature-lifecycle-persona-skills-with-enforced-phase-gate"></a>

## Entry 1 — 2026-10-29 — feat(init-repo): feature lifecycle persona skills with enforced phase gates

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

Working straight from idea to code without role changes led to fatigue, skipped thinking and chasing side issues. The team shares persona skills, reviews each other's work, generates every artefact with AI (no hand edits), and uses four agents in order of precedence: Claude, Codex, Kiro, opencode. Handoffs needed to be visible to colleagues, and phase order needed enforcing rather than relying on discipline.

## Decision

Ship the lifecycle as part of the per-repo `init-repo` kit rather than as a marketplace plugin, so every agent sees the same skills. GitHub issues are the status source of truth (a parent feature issue with one sub-issue per phase, or a single checklist issue in lite mode); files under `docs/features/<slug>/` hold content. All gate logic lives in one deterministic script invoked by both skills and CI, using only the `gh` CLI. Pushback reopens an earlier phase; explicit ADRs are allowed; the developer phase stops after the detailed plans; acceptance has a scripted walkthrough and an executable test in both local and deployed environments. CODEOWNERS and the admin merge override are kept as they are. Rejected: per-agent skill variants (drift), MCP-based GitHub access (not available in every agent or in Actions), and an issue-event workflow to re-run checks after pushback (deferred for simplicity).

## Consequences

Phase PRs in target repos must close their phase sub-issue and pass `feature-gate`; a PR closing two phases of one feature is blocked until split, and an unreadable closing reference fails closed (`gate-override` is the escape hatch). Known gaps left open: pushback does not re-run an already-green check, a PR can still edit `feature-gate.yml` itself, a kit update is gated by the old script on the base, `promote` is not idempotent after a partial failure, and lite-mode phase detection relies on branch naming. opencode sees byte-identical duplicate skills from two install paths.

<a id="entry-docs-add-mit-license-and-describe-the-skills-in-the-readme"></a>

## Entry 2 — 2026-10-29 — docs: add MIT license and describe the skills in the README

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The marketplace was private, so installing the plugin needed read access to the repo. It had no
licence, and its README said little about what each skill does. Opening it up needs both a
licence and a README a stranger can read.

## Decision

License the repository under MIT and make it public. The README now lists every skill with its
purpose. Branch protection stays as it is: one code-owner approval, `ai-fingerprint` required,
and `enforce_admins` off so the owner can override. Apache-2.0 was considered and not chosen,
because MIT is shorter and the project has no patent concerns.

## Consequences

Anyone can install, fork and reuse the plugin. The commit history, including author emails, is
now public. The `init-repo` dependency notes still assume local checkouts under
`~/RiderProjects`, with flags to override them.

<a id="entry-feat-lifecycle-slice-dev-plans-into-increments-with-a-stop-at-each-bound"></a>

## Entry 3 — 2026-11-10 — feat(lifecycle): slice dev plans into increments with a stop at each boundary

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The developer phase went straight from the accepted design to one plan and one build. On large features that made the plan PR hard to review, made long detailed plans harder for a small local model to execute, and gave the build no point where it could safely stop while leaving something working. Splitting detailed plans by layer (domain / application / infrastructure / API / web) made this worse, because nothing worked end to end until the last layer was done.

## Decision

Slice every feature by behaviour into increments that can each be deployed on their own, and run the build one increment per session with a stop at each boundary ("pencils down"). Small features are exempt below a threshold of about eight tasks. Rejected alternative: giving each increment its own build phase, PR and gate. That would mean changing the phase model in `feature.mjs` and the sub-issues, so for now the increment boundary is a checkpoint within the single dev-build phase.

## Consequences

Plans get an increment table, and plan reviews also approve the build order. Builds take more sessions, but each one leaves the system working. Increment boundaries are enforced through the skill and the exit criteria, not by the gate script, so that is left open: if it proves too loose, per-increment gating is the follow-up.

<a id="entry-doc-comments-stable-behaviour-ids-and-the-dev-plan-folder-in-the-init-re"></a>

## Entry 4 — 2026-11-23 — Doc comments, stable behaviour ids and the dev plan folder in the init-repo baseline

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The baseline said nothing about code comments, so agents wrote whatever comments they liked, and detailed plans asked only for "member-level comments" with no format. Separately, behaviour ids were regenerated freely when pushback reopened the analyst, so anything that referred to an id (tests, commits, and planned source-graph links) could silently point at the wrong behaviour after an amendment. The `feature-dev` wording also left it unclear whether a plan written without superpowers still belonged under `docs/superpowers/plans/`.

## Decision

Require doc comments on every public type and member in the language's standard doc-comment format, with XML doc comments for C#, and make detailed-plan interfaces use that format. Enforce this by instruction only; build enforcement was rejected as a breaking change for existing repositories. Make behaviour ids permanent once published: never renumbered or reused, retired rather than deleted, and referenced as `<slug>#B<n>` outside their feature. Keep `docs/superpowers/plans/` as the plan folder with or without superpowers; a neutral `docs/plans/` folder was tried and reverted to keep existing plan locations.

## Consequences

Generated repositories document public code consistently, and detailed plans show the expected comments to the models that execute them, but nothing fails a build when a comment is missing. Behaviour ids can now be cited from tests, commits and a source knowledge graph without going stale after amendments, at the cost of ids no longer being in order within a group. Existing repositories need their `AGENTS.md` and persona skills refreshed to get these rules. The plan folder keeps a superpowers-specific name even when superpowers is not used.

<a id="entry-feat-lifecycle-require-frontmatter-on-feature-artefacts-and-adrs"></a>

## Entry 5 — 2026-11-24 — feat(lifecycle): require frontmatter on feature artefacts and ADRs

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The persona skills generate a lot of Markdown, but nothing machine-readable ties a document to its feature, phase or inputs. ADR status lived in a bullet list that nothing checked. Adding frontmatter without anything that reads it would only create fields that decay. Putting phase progress in frontmatter would duplicate the issue state, which AGENTS.md treats as worse than no copy.

## Decision

Require frontmatter that holds only facts that never change on feature artefacts, and frontmatter with status on ADRs, the one status no issue tracks. Enforce both in `feature-gate` and in a local `check-frontmatter` command. Superpowers plans and detailed implementation plans are deliberately left without frontmatter: superpowers controls its own output, and the detailed-plan header format is already prescribed.

Rejected alternatives: a blanket "add frontmatter" instruction with no check, and progress fields (status, completion) in feature artefacts.

## Consequences

Artefacts can be traced to their feature and inputs by tooling, and an ADR's supersession is explicit. Existing features need their frontmatter added on the next PR that touches them. Whether a source actually exists, and whether its content matches, is deliberately not checked.

<a id="entry-feat-lifecycle-spec-kit-ideas-as-guidance-feature-analyze-quality-attrib"></a>

## Entry 6 — 2026-11-24 — feat(lifecycle): Spec Kit ideas as guidance: feature-analyze, quality attributes, priority

*Kind: product. Status: accepted.*

## Context

The exit criteria are ticked by the agent doing the work, and nothing checks the artefacts against each other, so drift between the vision, behaviours, architecture, plan and acceptance goes unnoticed until it becomes code. Several things were also left to the agent:
- the analyst's uncertainty list depended on what it happened to notice;
- non-functional requirements had no owner;
- increment order was decided at planning;
- nothing marked tasks whose order doesn't matter.

Spec Kit covers each of these. The owner's tooling principles rule out the usual way of enforcing them: low friction (nothing new may block) and readable documents (no fixed layouts for a checker).

## Decision

Adopt the ideas as guidance, with no enforcement.

- The consistency review is an advisory skill (`feature-analyze`), run when wanted and suggested once at the architect checkpoint.
- The analyst owns quality attributes and the user's acceptance proves them. Priority lives in the document body, because PR 12's frontmatter check rejects unknown keys.
- The `[P]` marker lives in feature-dev rather than the `AGENTS.md` task format, because `init-repo` overwrites the kit on every run but never rewrites an existing `AGENTS.md`.

Rejected alternatives:
- a `feature.mjs analyze` script or a CI step, because it would force fixed formats and could block;
- a review step at every checkpoint, which adds friction even when there's nothing to find;
- giving quality attributes to the product owner (too coarse) or the architect (the builder would decide what's required);
- putting `[P]` in both `AGENTS.md` and the skill, which leaves two copies of one rule.

## Consequences

- Drift and gaps can be found on demand, but nothing guarantees anyone looks.
- Quality attributes are traced and accepted like behaviours, without entering any gate.
- Increment order now follows the spec's priorities.
- Existing target repos get all of this on their next `init-repo` run, because the kit is overwritten.

Deliberately left open:
- whether P3 behaviours may be dropped (today priority only sets the order);
- whether every quality attribute can be checked in a local build;
- the deferred wording minors listed above.
